text: Light takes time to travel. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. Light from very distant [[@galaxies|galaxies]] has been travelling for billions of years. So when the James Webb Space Telescope catches that light, it sees those [[galaxy|galaxies]] as they were long ago, not as they are now.

Webb is the largest telescope ever sent into space. Its huge golden mirror can collect very faint light from galaxies that formed only a few hundred million years after the universe began. That makes it a kind of time machine, looking back across more than 13 billion years.

st.prompt: Why does looking at very distant galaxies mean looking into the past?

options.t: Their light took billions of years to reach us

st.reveal: Light travels fast but not instantly. Light from a galaxy 13 billion light-years away left it 13 billion years ago, so we see it as it was then.

Hubble is still working. The two telescopes see different kinds of light, Hubble mainly visible and ultraviolet, Webb mainly infrared, so astronomers often use them together to study the same objects.

sec.t:
Webb mostly sees [[infrared|infrared]] light, which lies just beyond red in the rainbow. Our eyes can't see it, though we feel some of it as warmth.

There are two big reasons to look in infrared. First, as the universe expands, light from the most distant galaxies gets stretched on its long journey, from visible colours into infrared. Second, infrared passes through clouds of dust that block ordinary light. That lets Webb peer inside [[@nebulae|dusty nebulas]] to watch stars being born.

Because Webb sees heat, its own warmth could drown out the faint glow of distant galaxies. So it must be very cold, below about −220 °C.

A sunshield the size of a tennis court, made of five thin layers, blocks heat from the Sun, Earth and Moon. One side faces the Sun and heats up to more than 80 °C. The other side stays colder than anywhere naturally found on Earth. Webb [[@spacecraft-move|orbits]] a point about 1.5 million km from Earth, roughly four times farther than the Moon, where it can keep the Sun, Earth and Moon behind its shield.

Webb launched on 25 December 2021, on a European Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in South America. Its first deep picture, released in July 2022, showed thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky about the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.

Since then, it has spotted some of the most distant galaxies ever seen. It has found [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] in the air of a planet around another star, one of many [[@exoplanets|exoplanets]] it studies. It has photographed star nurseries, dying stars and the planets of our own [[solar-system|solar system]] in new detail.

Webb is often called the successor to the [[@hubble|Hubble Space Telescope]], launched in 1990. Its mirror collects about six times as much light as Hubble's. But Hubble still works, and sees mostly visible and [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light. Together, the two give [[astronomer|astronomers]] a fuller picture of the universe, from nearby planets to the first galaxies.

text: India's vultures were poisoned by a [[@medicine-how|medicine]]. In the 1990s, farmers began giving sick cattle a cheap painkiller called diclofenac. When a treated animal died, traces of the drug stayed in its body. Vultures that ate the [[carcass|carcass]] suffered kidney failure and died, even from tiny amounts.

In the 1980s, vultures were among the most common big birds in India. By the mid-2000s, three [[species|species]] had fallen by more than 95%. The white-rumped vulture, once seen in huge flocks, dropped by more than 99%.

st.reveal: Farmers gave cattle a cheap painkiller called diclofenac. When a treated cow died soon after, traces of the drug stayed in its body. Vultures that fed on it suffered kidney failure, even from small amounts.

sec.t:
In the late 1990s, bird scientists such as Vibhu Prakash of the Bombay Natural History Society noticed that vultures were vanishing fast. Dead birds were found slumped on branches, their heads hanging down. Nesting colonies in Keoladeo National Park in Rajasthan went quiet.

At first, nobody knew why. Was it a virus? A [[pesticide|pesticide]]? Scientists tested every idea they could think of. In 2004, a team working in Pakistan, led by the American vet Lindsay Oaks, published the answer. The dead vultures had gout and kidney damage, and traces of diclofenac in their bodies.

sec.h: How a painkiller became a poison

sec.t:
Vultures have a job nobody else does as well. A flock can strip a dead cow to its bones within an hour. In a country with many millions of [[@cows-india|cattle]], they quietly cleaned up an enormous amount of dead meat.

When the vultures vanished, carcasses lay rotting for days. Stray dogs and rats moved in to feed, and their numbers grew. More dogs meant more dog bites and more cases of rabies. A 2024 study by two economists even estimated that the loss of vultures may have led to hundreds of thousands of extra human deaths, through dirtier water and more disease.

In Mumbai, the Parsi community had long laid their dead in Towers of Silence, where vultures did their natural work. With the birds gone, the community had to find new ways to keep this tradition going.

In 2006, India banned diclofenac for animals. Shops still sold human-sized bottles for use on cattle, so in 2015 the government limited the size of the bottles too. In 2023 it also banned two other animal painkillers, aceclofenac and ketoprofen, for the same reason.

Scientists set up breeding centres, starting with one at Pinjore in Haryana in 2001. Vultures breed slowly, laying one egg a year, so progress is slow. Some captive-bred birds have now been released into the wild, in areas where farmers and [[@jobs-vet|vets]] agree to use safer drugs, such as meloxicam.

A comeback is possible. In the USA, the California condor, a giant New World vulture, fell to just 27 birds in 1987. Careful breeding has brought it back to hundreds. In India, vultures were honoured long before scientists studied them. In the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], the vulture king Jatayu gave his life trying to rescue Sita. The [[@bald-eagle|bald eagle]] shows that birds can recover from a poison once people stop using it. Today's job is to give Jatayu's [[descendant|descendants]] the same chance.

text: Sea creatures glow by making light inside their bodies, a trick called [[bioluminescence|bioluminescence]]. A chemical called luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped along by an [[enzyme|enzyme]], and [[@how-glow-sticks|the energy comes out as light instead of heat]]. It is the same basic idea that lights up [[@fireflies|fireflies]] on a summer evening.

In the dark ocean, light is a powerful tool. Animals glow to find food, to hide, to scare off attackers and to find mates. A 2017 study by scientists in California found that about three out of every four animals they filmed in the deep sea could make light. Glowing is not rare down there. It is normal.

st.prompt: Most glowing sea creatures make blue light. Why blue?

options.t: Blue light travels farthest through seawater
Blue is the only colour animals can make

st.reveal: Seawater soaks up red and yellow light within a few metres, but blue light travels much farther. Many deep-sea animals can only see blue, so that is the colour that works best for signalling. A few fish make red light as a secret beam that their prey can't see.

src: Martini S. & Haddock S.H.D. (2017) Quantification of bioluminescence from the surface to the deep sea. Scientific Reports 7.

d.try: In a dark room, shine a torch through a clear glass of water, then add a few drops of milk and shine it again. Notice how the light spreads and glows in the cloudy water. Divers see something similar when glowing plankton light up the water around them.
myth: Glowing waves are a sign that the sea is clean and healthy.

Glowing waves are often caused by huge blooms of plankton. Big blooms can be fed by nutrients washing in from farms and sewage, and can use up oxygen that fish need. They are beautiful, but not always good news.

Most common colour in the sea

sec.t:
You don't need a submarine to see bioluminescence. On some nights, tiny single-celled [[plankton|plankton]] called dinoflagellates fill coastal waters. Each one flashes when the water around it is disturbed. When a wave breaks or a person wades in, millions flash together and the water glows blue. Footprints in wet sand can sparkle, and a hand swept through the water leaves a trail like a [[comet|comet]]. The glow fades within seconds, then flares again with the next splash.

In India, glowing waves have been seen on beaches in [[@goa|Goa]], Karnataka, Kerala, Mumbai, Chennai and [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]]. In [[@puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]], Mosquito Bay on the island of Vieques is famous as one of the brightest glowing bays in the world. Its narrow mouth keeps the plankton trapped inside, and nearby mangroves feed them.

Glowing sea animals have changed medicine. In the 1960s, the Japanese scientist Osamu Shimomura studied a glowing jellyfish from the coast of Washington state in the United States. He found a [[protein|protein]] in it that glows green under blue light.

Other scientists later learned to attach this green protein to cells and genes, so they could see exactly where those parts were working inside living things. It became one of the most widely used tools in biology, helping researchers watch nerve cells grow and cancer cells spread. In 2008, Shimomura and two American scientists, Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien, shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.

Bioluminescence also helps explorers. The American scientist Edith Widder designed a camera that films using red light, which most deep-sea animals cannot see, so they behave normally. She also built an electronic lure that copies the glowing alarm of a jellyfish. In 2012, it helped a team film a living giant squid in its home waters off Japan for the first time.

Even on land, a few living things glow, including some mushrooms and fungi on rotting wood. But the ocean is where living light really rules. Far below the reach of the Sun, nearly all the light there is comes from animals.

text: An electric eel's body is mostly a living battery. Most of its long tail is packed with thousands of flat cells called electrocytes, stacked in rows like coins. Each cell can make only a small voltage, a fraction of a volt. But when the eel's brain sends a signal, they all fire at the same instant, and their voltages add up.

Small, weak pulses help the eel sense its surroundings in muddy water. Big, strong pulses stun prey and frighten enemies. In 2019, scientists measured one [[species|species]], Volta's electric eel, firing 860 volts, the strongest shock known from any animal.

st.prompt: How does an electric eel build up a shock big enough to stun a fish?

options.t: Thousands of special cells fire at once, adding their small voltages together
It rubs its skin on rocks to build static

st.reveal: Each electric cell makes only a tiny voltage, about as much as a fraction of a small battery. Thousands stacked in rows fire together, and their voltages add up, the same way batteries in a torch add up.

sec.t:
Electric eels live in the slow rivers and swamps of the [[@brazil-amazon|Amazon]] and Orinoco in South America. They grow up to about 2.5 m long, as long as a small car, and look like snakes. But they are knifefish, cousins of catfish and carp, not true eels.

They have a strange habit. Their muddy rivers hold little oxygen, so electric eels swim up every few minutes to gulp air. Most of their oxygen comes from air breathed through their mouths, and an eel kept underwater for too long will drown.

Scientists have filmed electric eels doing clever things. When a fish hides, an eel can send out a quick double pulse. The jolt makes the hidden fish's muscles twitch, giving away its position. Then the eel blasts it with a full volley and gulps it down.

An eel can also curl around struggling prey, bringing its head and tail close together, which concentrates the shock. In 2021, scientists in Brazil reported Volta's electric eels hunting in a group of about 100, herding small fish into a ball before attacking together. Until then, people thought electric eels always hunted alone.

In 1800, the explorer Alexander von Humboldt described electric eels in Venezuela leaping from the water to shock horses driven into a pool. For two centuries, many scientists doubted the story. In 2016, a [[biologist|biologist]] in the USA showed that eels really do leap out and press their chins against a threat, sending the shock straight into it.

A shock from a big eel can knock a person down, and in rare cases people have drowned after being stunned. How the eel avoids shocking itself is not fully understood, though fatty tissue around its organs may work a little like the rubber coating on a wire. They are best admired from a distance.

In 1800, the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta built the first battery, a stack of metal discs and wet cardboard. He had been studying electric fish, and he called his invention an "artificial electric organ". Today, the strongest eel species is named after him, and his wobbly stack of discs was the ancestor of every [[@batteries-history|battery]] in your home.

Electric eels are not the only animals that use electricity. Sharks and rays sense the faint electric fields of hidden prey, and the [[@power-platypus|platypus]] hunts with its eyes closed, using its bill to feel the tiny electric signals of shrimp.

text: Wombats are stocky, burrowing animals from Australia, about the size of a medium dog. They are the only animals known to make poop shaped like cubes, with flat sides and fairly sharp corners.

For a long time, nobody knew how. In 2018, a team of scientists in the USA and Australia studied the guts of wombats that had been killed on roads. They found that the cubes form inside the last part of the intestine. That part of the gut wall has bands that are stiff and bands that are stretchy. As dry poop is squeezed along, the stretchy bands push in harder, carving flat faces, while the stiff bands make corners.
Why wombats make cubes is less certain. The best idea is that they use them as signposts, and cubes do not roll away.

st.prompt: Where in a wombat's body do the cubes get their shape?

options.t: Near the end of the intestine, where the gut wall has stiff and stretchy bands

In the stomach, before food is digested

st.reveal: Scientists found that the last part of a wombat's intestine has bands of stiffer and stretchier wall. As the poop dries and is squeezed along, the uneven walls press it into corners and flat sides, over many hours.

Squeeze both gently in your hands. Notice how the bands change the shape where the balloon pushes out. Wombat guts work on a similar idea.

This story spread widely online, but there is no evidence wombats deliberately rescued anyone. Other animals did shelter in wombat burrows, which stayed cooler than the burning ground, so the burrows really did help.

up to about two weeks to pass through
Ig Nobel Prize for the cube research

sec.t:
Wombats eat tough grasses, roots and bark. To get every bit of goodness out, they digest very slowly. Food can take up to about two weeks to pass through a wombat, much longer than in humans, who usually take one to three days.

All that time lets the gut soak up almost all the water. So wombat poop comes out very dry and firm, which helps the cubes keep their shape. Each cube is about 2 cm across, roughly the size of a sugar cube or a big dice.

A single wombat can drop around 80 to 100 of them in one night.

The engineer Patricia Yang and her colleagues did something careful and slightly gross. They compared wombat intestines with pig intestines, stretched them like long balloons and measured how stiff the walls were. They then built computer models of the squeezing.

Their findings won the 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in physics. These prizes, handed out for many years at Harvard University, honour research that first makes people laugh, then makes them think. The team suggested factories could one day learn from wombats, because making cubes usually needs moulds or cutting, and wombats do it with soft tissue.

[[@shapes-3d|Cubes]] are rare in nature. Salt crystals make them, and so do some minerals, but living things almost never produce them.

Wombats are tough. They have strong legs and long claws for digging burrows that can run for tens of metres. A female's pouch faces backwards, towards her hind legs. That way, when she digs, soil does not fly into the pouch and onto her baby, called a joey.

Their rump is covered by a hard plate of bone and [[cartilage|cartilage]] under thick skin. When chased into a burrow, a wombat may block the entrance with its bottom, which is very hard for a [[predator|predator]] to bite. Despite their chunky shape, wombats can run at about 40 km/h for short bursts, about as fast as a top human sprinter.

During the huge [[@forest-fires|bushfires]] in Australia in 2019 and 2020, stories spread online that wombats had herded other animals into their burrows to save them. That did not happen on purpose. But wombat burrows stayed cooler and safer than the burning ground, and other animals did use them to shelter.

Wombats share their home country with other unusual [[marsupial|marsupials]], animals that carry their babies in pouches. One of them, the [[@wild-koala|koala]], spends most of its life asleep, for a reason that also comes down to a very slow, very picky gut.

text: Light adds up. Paint takes away. That one idea explains the puzzle.

Red, green and blue lights shone together on a white wall make white. Your [[@made-phone-screens|phone screen]] builds every colour from tiny red, green and blue dots, called [[@pixels|pixels]], switched on in different amounts.

Paint works the other way. A paint looks red because it soaks up most of the other colours in light and bounces red back to your eyes. Mix two paints and each one soaks up its share, so less light escapes. Mix them all and almost nothing bright is left: muddy brown or dark grey.
That's why printers use cyan, magenta and yellow ink, while screens use red, green and blue light.

quiz.prompt: A red light and a green light shine on the same spot of a white wall. What colour do you see?
quiz.reveal: Light adds up. Red light excites your eye's red-sensing cones and green light excites the green ones. Your brain reads that mix as yellow, even though there is no yellow light at all.

src: Hunt R.W.G. (2004) The Reproduction of Colour, 6th ed. Wiley.
Exploratorium, ‘Colored Shadows’ and additive colour.

d.try: Make a colour spinner. Take a small paper plate, colour it in equal slices of red, green and blue, and ask an adult to push a short pencil through the centre. Spin it like a top. The colours blur together in your eyes and the disc looks pale and greyish, because your eyes are mixing light, not paint.
myth: The primary colours are red, yellow and blue, and that's that.
Red, yellow and blue is a traditional set for mixing paint. For light, the main colours are red, green and blue, and printers use cyan, magenta and yellow. No set of three can make every colour.
facts: adds colours; mixing paint takes them away

sec.t:
Around 1666, [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]] let a thin beam of sunlight pass through a glass [[prism|prism]] in a darkened room. It spread into a band of colours, like a [[@rainbow-how|rainbow]]. Then he used a second prism to squeeze the colours back together, and they made white light again.

So white is not "no colour". It is all the colours of visible light arriving at once. A red apple looks red because its skin swallows most of those colours and sends back mainly red. In a room lit only by blue light, the same apple looks almost black, because there is no red light for it to bounce back.

Each [[pigment|pigment]] is a powder that absorbs some colours and reflects the rest. Yellow paint swallows mostly blue light. Cyan, a greenish blue, swallows mostly red. Mix them, and between them they swallow both red and blue, so mainly green escapes. That's why yellow and blue make green in your paintbox.

Add more pigments and each one steals a bit more light. Stir red, yellow, blue and everything else together, and very little is reflected. You get a dull brown. Painters call this "mud", and art teachers spend years warning students to keep their brushes clean.

[[@printers|A colour printer]] holds cyan, magenta and yellow ink, plus black, often labelled CMYK. Tiny dots of the three colours overlap on white paper to make thousands of shades. Black is added because the three together make a murky dark brown, not a crisp black, and black ink is cheaper.

Artists learned these rules long before anyone could explain them. The painters of [[@ajanta-colours|Ajanta]] mixed earth colours by eye and by experience. Stage lights in a school hall follow light's rules instead. Point red, green and blue spotlights at the same place and the overlap turns white, while the shadow of a person standing in front splits into a row of coloured silhouettes.

text: Kangra painting is a style of small, delicate pictures made in the hill kingdoms of the western Himalaya, mainly in the late 1700s and early 1800s. It is named after Kangra, a kingdom in what is now Himachal Pradesh, where it reached its peak under Raja Sansar Chand. It belongs to the wider family of Pahari, or "hill", painting, which is part of [[@rajput-painting|Rajput painting]].

Kangra paintings are known for soft colours, flowing lines and graceful figures with gentle faces. Most tell love stories of Radha and Krishna, set in green countryside with rivers, banana trees and distant hills. They feel calm and poetic, quite unlike the bold, bright pictures made in many Rajasthani courts.

st.reveal: In Indian poetry the monsoon is the season of longing, when travellers try to return home. Kangra artists painted swirling dark clouds, thin zigzags of gold lightning, cranes flying in a line and peacocks calling, all to show a feeling of missing someone.

d.try: Choose a feeling, like missing a friend or waiting for good news, and paint or draw a small landscape that shows it without any people. Use weather, trees, birds and colours to carry the mood. Kangra painters did the same with rain clouds, lightning and peacocks.
myth: Miniature paintings were painted by one artist working alone.

Many Kangra paintings were made by workshops. A master might draw the outline, while family members prepared paper, ground colours, painted backgrounds or added gold. Skills passed down through families for generations.

sec.t:
Much of the Kangra style grew out of one family from Guler, a small state close to Kangra. The painter Pandit Seu had two famous sons, Manaku and Nainsukh. Nainsukh worked for a prince in Jasrota and painted lively scenes from court life, including the prince listening to music, smoking a hookah and watching dancers.

The next generation, sons and nephews of these brothers, carried the style further. Working for rulers including Sansar Chand, they painted great sets of pictures for the Gita Govinda and the Bhagavata Purana. The art historian B. N. Goswamy spent years tracing this family through old records, including notes left by pilgrims at Haridwar.

Kangra painters looked closely at the land around them. You can spot the curving river Beas, the layered hills of the Dhauladhar range, mango and banana trees and village huts with sloping roofs. Night scenes glow with moonlight, and storm scenes have thin lines of real gold for lightning.

Colours were made from minerals and plants, ground by hand and mixed with gum. Fine brushes used a few hairs from a squirrel's tail. Artists built up layers so thin that the paper underneath seems to glow through, and polished the finished painting with a smooth stone. Hill painters learned a lot from [[@mughal-miniatures|Mughal miniatures]], especially the fine shading and the careful, natural-looking faces, and then made the style their own.

sec.h: A court that rose and fell
sec.t:
Raja Sansar Chand ruled Kangra from 1775 to 1823 and loved art, music and poetry. He kept many painters at his court in Tira Sujanpur and Nadaun. For a time, his kingdom was the strongest in the hills.

Then troubles came. Gurkha armies from Nepal attacked, and in 1809 the Sikh ruler [[@ranjit-singh|Ranjit Singh]] took Kangra Fort. Later the British took control of the area. Without rich patrons, the painters scattered or turned to cheaper work.

In 1905, a powerful [[@earthquakes|earthquake]] shook Kangra and destroyed much of the town and its old fort. Many paintings had already left the region, and today the best collections are in museums in Chandigarh, New Delhi, Chamba, London and Boston.

Some artists in Himachal Pradesh still paint in the Kangra style, using natural colours and fine brushes, and teach young painters to carry it on. Their pictures sell to visitors in Dharamshala and Kangra, a short drive from the hills the old masters painted.

text: People fight forest fires mainly by taking away what a fire needs to burn. Every fire needs three things: heat, fuel and oxygen. Firefighters cool flames with water, smother them with soil, and above all remove the fuel in front of the fire.

On the ground, crews dig long strips of bare earth called fire lines. From the air, planes and helicopters drop water or a red chemical that slows burning. Sometimes crews deliberately burn a strip ahead of the fire, so the big blaze reaches ground already burned. Modern teams also use weather forecasts and satellites to predict where a fire will run next.

st.prompt: Firefighters dig a long strip of bare earth, scraped clear of leaves and twigs, in front of a wildfire. Why?

options.t: To let water soak into the ground faster

Many forests and grasslands evolved with fire. Small, cool fires clear dead wood and help some seeds sprout. Some pine cones only open after fire. Putting out every small fire can let fuel pile up until a huge one breaks out.

sec.t:
The most important tool in many wildfires is a hand tool. Crews of about 20 people, called hotshot crews in the USA, cut through brush and scrape the ground down to bare soil. A fire line can stretch for kilometres.

Their favourite tool is the Pulaski, half axe and half hoe. It was designed by Ed Pulaski, a forest ranger in Idaho. In 1910 a giant fire known as the Big Burn swept across the northwestern USA. Pulaski led his crew of about 45 men into an old mine tunnel and refused to let anyone run back out into the flames. Most of them survived.

Some fires start from lightning in wild mountains far from any road. In the USA, smokejumpers reach them by parachute. The first jump onto a fire was in 1940. Today, jumpers leap from planes with tools, food and water dropped alongside them.

Once on the ground, they may work for days before hiking out to a road. A [[@parachutes|parachute]] gets them in. Their own legs get them out, often carrying 50 kg of gear.

India's forests catch fire most often between February and June, when leaves are dry and the [[monsoon|monsoon]] hasn't arrived. The Forest Survey of India uses [[@satellites-help|satellites]] that pass overhead and detect hot spots. Alerts go by text message and email to forest staff near each fire, often within hours.

In the Himalaya, chir pine needles carpet the ground and burn very easily. Many villages have their own forest councils. Villagers clear needles, beat out small flames with green branches and keep watch, carrying on a tradition of caring for forests seen in the [[@chipko|Chipko movement]].

A backburn is a fire set on purpose by firefighters. They light it along a road or fire line, burning towards the main fire. When the two meet, there is nothing left to burn. It takes skill, because a shift in the wind can make a backburn dangerous. Crews watch the weather constantly, and US wildland firefighters carry a folding fire shelter, a foil tent to crawl under if flames ever come too close.

Some fire is even good. Many Aboriginal Australians and Native American nations have long used small, cool fires to clear undergrowth. Scientists now study these traditions to prevent huge blazes. In the USA, Smokey Bear has reminded people since 1944 that most wildfires are started by humans. Why flames spread the way they do comes down to the chemistry of [[@fire-burns|how fire burns]].

text: For most of history, women in most countries could not vote, own much property in their own name or study at university. Laws and customs treated them as belonging to their fathers, then their husbands.

That changed bit by bit, over about two centuries, because women organised. They wrote petitions, marched, went on hunger strikes, went to court and stood for election. Some men supported them. The fight looked different in every country, and in many ways it is still going on. Today, most [[constitution|constitutions]], including [[@constitution|India's]], promise equal rights for women and men.

sec.h: The long march for the vote

sec.t:
In India, reform began with campaigns against child marriage and for girls' education. [[@savitribai-phule|Savitribai Phule]] opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848. In 1886, Anandibai Joshi graduated from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania, becoming one of the first Indian women trained in Western medicine.

Women joined the freedom struggle in large numbers. [[@sarojini-naidu|Sarojini Naidu]] became the first Indian woman president of the Indian National Congress in 1925, and in 1930 she led protesters at Dharasana during the salt protests. When the Constitution came into force in 1950, every adult woman got the vote at the same moment as every man. Fifteen women were members of the [[@constituent-assembly|Constituent Assembly]] that wrote it.

Voting was a start. Women also fought for equal pay, for the right to [[inherit|inherit]] and for protection from violence. In the USA, the Equal Pay Act of 1963 made it illegal to pay women less for the same work. A 1972 law called Title IX banned sex discrimination in schools that get [[federal|federal]] money, and girls' sports teams grew fast.

In India, a 2005 change to the law gave Hindu daughters the same right as sons to inherit family property. Since 1993, at least a third of village council seats have been reserved for women.

Around the world, women still earn less than men on average, and hold fewer seats in [[parliament|parliaments]] and fewer top jobs. In some places, girls are kept out of school altogether, which is why [[@malala|Malala Yousafzai]] became famous for speaking up.

Progress has also come from people who simply did the work. Indian women scientists helped send probes to Mars and the Moon, and in the 1960s, Black American women did the maths for NASA's early crewed flights. Each first made the next one easier.

text: Indian cinema grew out of traditions where stories were sung and danced, like folk theatre.

Songs show feelings, dreams and celebrations in a way words alone can't. A song can show a couple falling in love across a whole season, or a hero's sorrow, in four minutes. They also give a long film breaks, like the songs in a stage show.
Playback singers record the songs, and actors lip-sync on screen. Songs are often released before the film, and a hit soundtrack can fill cinema halls.

sec.t:
[[@storytelling-india|Indian storytelling]] has long mixed words, music and dance. Sanskrit drama, temple performances, the Ramlila and village folk theatre all used song. In the 1800s, Parsi theatre companies toured India with plays full of music, drama and spectacle. Early filmmakers grew up watching them.

So when films learned to talk, it seemed natural for them to sing. *Alam Ara*, India's first talking film, made by Ardeshir Irani in 1931, had seven songs. A year later, a film called *Indrasabha* had around 70. Audiences loved them.

In the early 1950s, India's information minister decided film songs were too low-class for [[@radio-india|All India Radio]], and they were largely taken off the air. Listeners simply retuned to Radio Ceylon, broadcasting from Colombo in [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]]. Its weekly countdown, *Binaca Geetmala*, presented by Ameen Sayani, drew huge audiences from 1952.

All India Radio soon gave in and launched Vividh Bharati in 1957, packed with film music. Songs became the soundtrack of daily life: in tea stalls, buses and wedding processions.

Today a film song is usually recorded months before it is filmed. The [[@film-music-composers|composer]], lyricist and singer work in a studio, often recording each instrument and voice separately. Then the director and a choreographer plan the dance, and the actors learn to mime every word in time with the recording.

Songs are often shot in beautiful places far from the story's setting. Director Yash Chopra filmed so many songs in the Swiss Alps that Indian tourists began visiting the same valleys.

Music directors became stars too. S.D. Burman and his son R.D. Burman mixed Indian folk with jazz and rock. Ilaiyaraaja shaped Tamil film music with orchestras. [[@ar-rahman|A.R. Rahman]] used synthesisers and computers to create new sounds in the 1990s, and won two Oscars in 2009 for *Slumdog Millionaire*.

In 2023, "Naatu Naatu" from the Telugu film *RRR*, composed by M.M. Keeravani, became the first song from an Indian film to win the Oscar for Best Original Song.

[[@hollywood|Hollywood]] once made many musicals, like *The Wizard of Oz* in 1939 and *Singin' in the Rain* in 1952, but they became less common. Indian cinema kept singing. Today some films have fewer songs, or play them in the background instead of having stars dance. But songs still carry stories, and still give listeners [[@body-music-chills|the shivers]] that scientists link to [[@music-goosebumps|music and emotion]].

text: The Grammy Awards, usually called the Grammys, are among the world's best-known music prizes. They're given each year in the United States by the Recording Academy, an organisation of people who make music, such as singers, songwriters, producers and sound engineers.

There are more than 90 categories, covering pop, rock, rap, jazz, classical, country, music for children and "global music" from around the world. The winners receive a small gold gramophone trophy. The first ceremony was held in 1959, and the show is now a big television event every February.

sec.t:
Record companies and artists first submit music released during the past year. Members of the Recording Academy then vote to choose the nominees, usually five to eight in each category. Members vote again to pick the winner. Accountants count the ballots in secret.

Members are meant to vote only in areas they know well, so a jazz drummer might vote in jazz categories but not in classical. Many people assume sales decide the result. They don't. A huge hit can lose to a quieter album that musicians admire, unlike [[@music-charts|music charts]], which are based on sales and streams.

[[@ravi-shankar|Ravi Shankar]], the sitar master, won his first Grammy in 1967 for *West Meets East*, an album he made with the violinist Yehudi Menuhin. His daughter Anoushka Shankar has been nominated many times.

In 2010 [[@ar-rahman|A.R. Rahman]] won two Grammys for the music of *Slumdog Millionaire*. Bengaluru composer Ricky Kej has won several, the first in 2015. And at the 2024 ceremony, Zakir Hussain, the great [[@tabla|tabla]] player, won three Grammys in one night. One was for *This Moment*, an album by the fusion band Shakti, whose members include Hussain, singer Shankar Mahadevan and guitarist John McLaughlin.

The trophy is shaped like a gramophone, an early machine for playing records. It had a wide horn to make the sound louder. The name Grammy comes from the same word. In the early days of [[@sound-recording|sound recording]], the gramophone helped turn music into something people could buy and play at home.

Each trophy is made by hand in a workshop in Colorado. It takes many hours to cast, polish and plate in gold. Winners don't usually get their own engraved trophy on the night. They hold a stand-in on stage, and the finished one arrives weeks later with their name on it.

The Grammys aren't the only music prizes. Britain has the Brit Awards. India's Filmfare Awards, started in 1954, include prizes for film music and playback singing, and the National Film Awards honour the best composers and singers every year.

The Grammys also face criticism. Some artists have said that Black musicians, women and non-English singers have too often been overlooked in the top categories. The Academy has added new members and categories, including one for African music performance in 2024. Plenty of musicians still say the real prize is a song people keep singing years later.

text: A singing talent show is a contest on television. Ordinary people audition, judges pick the best, and over many weeks singers are knocked out until one wins. In the later rounds, viewers usually vote by phone, text message or app to keep their favourites in.

Behind the scenes, there's far more going on. Producers hold early auditions away from the cameras, pick contestants with good voices and interesting stories, and edit hours of footage into a tight show. It's a real singing contest, and also a TV programme built to keep you watching.

Most episodes are recorded earlier and edited. Producers choose which singers and stories to show, and contestants usually pass several rounds off-camera before meeting the judges. Some finals do have live public voting.

sec.t:
Talent contests are old. American radio shows ran amateur contests in the 1930s and 1940s, and Indian radio and TV had singing competitions for children and adults.

In India, Zee TV's Sa Re Ga Ma began in 1995, hosted for several years by the singer Sonu Nigam. It later became Sa Re Ga Ma Pa and spawned a children's version, Li'l Champs.

In 2001, a British show called Pop Idol added judges with sharp tongues and votes from viewers at home. American Idol followed in 2002, and Kelly Clarkson won the first season. Indian Idol began on Sony TV in 2004, and its first winner was Abhijeet Sawant.

First come mass auditions, often in several cities. Thousands of people queue, sometimes overnight, but most are turned away by producers before the famous judges see them. The few who appear on TV have already passed earlier rounds.

Next come theatre or studio rounds, where singers sing with a band, then in groups or duets. Finally the live shows begin. Each week, contestants sing, judges comment, and viewers vote. The singer with the fewest votes is usually sent home.

Judges are usually famous singers, composers or producers. Their job is partly to coach: they suggest songs, point out weak notes and tell a nervous singer to slow down. Some are kind, some are harsh, and their arguments are part of the fun. Producers know this, and choose judges who will clash.

Contestants' life stories are told in short films between songs. A singer who supports their family, or who travelled from a small village, gets a lot of attention. Critics say this can matter more than the [[@singing|singing]] itself.

Children's versions are very popular, but some people worry about the pressure. Young contestants practise for hours, face public rejection, and may become famous overnight, then forgotten.

Some show winners went on to long careers. Kelly Clarkson became a major star. Many Indian playback singers, including Shreya Ghoshal, first came to national attention on TV singing contests. Others went back to ordinary life, which is not always a bad thing. Training your [[@voice|voice]] in front of a crowd teaches skills that last, whether or not you win.

text: The famous plastic toy brick was made by LEGO, a company in Billund, Denmark. A carpenter named Ole Kirk Christiansen started it in 1932, making wooden toys. In 1949 the company began making plastic bricks. In 1958 it patented the design that clicks together so well today, with studs on top and hollow tubes underneath.

But LEGO didn't come up with the very first interlocking brick. A British inventor, Hilary Fisher Page, made Kiddicraft Self-Locking Building Bricks in the 1940s. LEGO's early bricks were closely based on them. Toy blocks of wood, stone and clay go back thousands of years before that.

sec.t:
Ole Kirk Christiansen was a carpenter in a small Danish village. In the 1930s, times were hard and few people were buying furniture. So he started making wooden toys: yo-yos, cars and a popular [[@pop-rubber-duck|pull-along duck]].

In 1934 he named the company LEGO, from the Danish words *leg godt*, meaning "play well". A favourite story says his son Godtfred once saved money by using cheap varnish on some ducks, and Ole Kirk made him go back and fix every one. The motto "only the best is good enough" was painted on the workshop wall.

The answer was hidden underneath. In 1958 LEGO added hollow tubes inside each brick. When you press a brick down, the studs below squeeze between the tubes and the walls and hold firm. The [[@patents|patent]] was filed on 28 January 1958.

A brick made in 1958 still fits a brick made today. Modern LEGO bricks are moulded so precisely that only about 18 in every million fail the company's quality checks. They're made from a tough plastic called ABS, which keeps its shape for decades.

Bricks combine in staggering numbers. Two 2x4 bricks of one colour can join in 24 ways. Three give 1,060 ways. In 2005, a mathematician at the University of Copenhagen, Søren Eilers, worked out that six bricks give 915,103,765 ways. With more bricks, the counts get so [[@big-numbers|big]] that even computers struggle.

This is the same sort of maths behind codes and puzzles. Each extra piece multiplies the choices, so small kits can lead to endless builds.

sec.h: Bricks, logs and blocks around the world
sec.t:
LEGO wasn't alone. In 1916, John Lloyd Wright, a son of the famous American architect [[@frank-lloyd-wright|Frank Lloyd Wright]], invented Lincoln Logs, notched wooden logs for building cabins. Britain had Meccano, metal strips with bolts, from the early 1900s.

In India, the town of Channapatna in Karnataka has made bright lacquered wooden toys for about 200 years, including stacking rings and spinning tops. Kids everywhere have always loved building things, knocking them down and building them again.

Today LEGO is one of the biggest toy companies in the world. Legoland parks in Denmark, the US, Japan and elsewhere are built from millions of bricks. In 2000, the British Association of Toy Retailers named LEGO the "Toy of the Century".

Brick building has also gone digital. Minecraft lets players build whole worlds from blocks on a screen, and many children use [[@minecraft-coding|Minecraft]] to learn the basics of coding.

text: Each hair on your head grows from a tiny pit in your skin called a [[follicle|follicle]]. Inside the follicle live [[pigment|pigment]] cells. As the hair grows, these cells pump colour, called [[melanin|melanin]], into it. Lots of dark melanin makes black or brown hair, and a reddish kind gives red and golden shades.

As people get older, the pigment cells in some follicles slowly stop working. The hairs from those follicles grow out with no colour, so they look white or silvery. Mixed with the dark hairs still growing, the overall effect looks grey. Most people find their first grey hairs in their thirties, but some go grey in their twenties and others hardly at all before sixty.

The stem cells that wander off
sec.t:
Pigment cells don't last forever. The follicle keeps a store of young "stem cells" that can turn into new pigment cells each time a hair starts to grow. In greying hair, this store runs low.

Research in mice has offered some clues. A 2023 study found that these stem cells normally move between two zones in the follicle, but as hairs age, many get stuck in one zone where they can't do their job. Other work suggests chemical wear and tear builds up in the follicle over time. Scientists are still piecing together how these ideas fit, and how well the mouse results match people.

The biggest clue to when you'll go grey is your family. If your parents and grandparents greyed early, you probably will too, because [[@genes-family|genes]] strongly shape the timing. Ancestry matters as well. On average, people of European descent tend to start greying a few years earlier than people of Asian or African descent, though there is a lot of overlap.

An old saying claimed that half of all people are half grey by age 50. A 2012 study of thousands of people across many countries found that figure was far too high. Most 50-year-olds in the study had much less grey than that.

People aren't the only ones who go grey. Many dogs get white hairs around their muzzles as they age, and older horses can grey around the eyes. In mountain gorillas, adult males grow a patch of silver hair on their backs, which is why they're called silverbacks, though that is a sign of being grown up rather than old.

Grey hairs often feel different from dark ones. Many people find them coarser, wirier or curlier. Scientists think the follicles change in other ways as they age, so the hair they make may be shaped differently as well as lacking colour.

People have long said that [[@stress|stress]] turns hair grey. In 2020, scientists at Harvard found that in mice, sudden stress made nerves in the skin release a chemical that used up the pigment stem cells for good. A 2021 study of people found that a few grey hairs regained some colour after a stressful period ended.

So stress may speed greying for some people, but it is far from the main cause. Going grey very young can sometimes be linked to low [[vitamin|vitamin]] B12 or thyroid problems, so it is worth mentioning to a doctor. Many people simply enjoy their grey, while others colour it with dyes or plant pastes like [[@mehendi|henna]]. Either way, greying is a normal part of [[@ageing|ageing]].

text: Digestion starts before you swallow. Your [[@teeth|teeth]] cut and grind the food, and [[@gross-saliva|saliva]] begins to break down [[starch|starch]]. Then a muscular tube called the oesophagus squeezes each mouthful down to your stomach.

The stomach churns food with [[acid|acid]] and [[enzyme|enzymes]] into a thick soup. Bit by bit, it squirts this into the small intestine, where most of the useful parts are pulled out and carried away by the blood. What's left moves into the large intestine, which soaks up water. The rest leaves your body as poo, usually one to three days after you ate.

st.prompt: Where in your body does most of the goodness from food actually soak into your blood?
st.reveal: The stomach mashes and starts breaking food down, but most nutrients pass into the blood through the walls of the small intestine. Its inside is covered in millions of tiny finger-like bumps that give it a huge surface.

Your body can't digest gum, but it doesn't get stuck. It moves through your gut and comes out within a few days, like other things you can't digest. Swallowing a lot of gum at once is still not a good idea.

sec.t:
Food doesn't fall down your gut. Rings of [[@muscles|muscle]] along the tube tighten one after another, pushing food forward the way you push toothpaste up a tube. This wave is called peristalsis. It's why [[@space-food|astronauts]] can swallow while floating, and why your gut works when you lie down.

At the top of your windpipe there is a small flap that closes when you swallow, so food goes down the right pipe. When it doesn't close in time, you cough hard to clear it.

An adult stomach can hold about a litre of food comfortably and stretch to hold more. Its walls make hydrochloric acid, strong enough to kill many germs and to start breaking down [[protein|proteins]]. So why doesn't the stomach digest itself? It coats its lining in thick [[mucus|mucus]], and it replaces the cells of its inner surface every few days.

Much of what we know about the stomach comes from one strange accident. In 1822, a young fur trader in Michigan, Alexis St. Martin, was shot by accident. He survived, but the wound left a hole into his stomach. An army doctor, William Beaumont, spent years dropping food on strings through the hole and pulling it out to see how it had changed.

He also drew out some of the stomach's juice and kept it in a warm jar with pieces of meat. The meat still broke down, slowly, with no stomach around it. That helped show that digestion is mostly chemistry, with squashing and grinding as helpers. Beaumont published his results in 1833, and doctors still mention his notes today.

{{story:cooking-science}}

The small intestine is coiled up in your belly, but stretched out it would be about 6 metres long, longer than a car. Your [[@liver|liver]] sends bile into it to break fat into tiny droplets, and the pancreas adds more enzymes. The inside wall is covered in millions of tiny bumps called villi, like the threads on a towel. They give it a huge surface for soaking up sugars, fats, [[@vitamins|vitamins]] and building blocks of protein.

The large intestine is wider but shorter, about 1.5 metres. Here the body takes back most of the water, so you don't dry out. This part is home to trillions of [[@microbes-friendly|friendly microbes]]. They eat the fibre that you can't digest, such as the skins of fruit and the husks of grains, and make some useful [[vitamin|vitamins]] in return.

Fibre also keeps everything moving. A meal of dal, rice and vegetables gives your gut [[microbe|microbes]] plenty to work on. When food passes through too quickly, the body can't take back enough water, and that is diarrhoea. When it moves too slowly, too much water is removed, and that is constipation.

text: In 1991, India changed the way its [[economy|economy]] worked. For about 40 years, the government had controlled much of business. Companies needed licences to start, grow or make new products, and [[import|imports]] were tightly limited.

That summer, India faced a money crisis. It had almost run out of foreign [[currency|currency]] to pay for oil and other imports. Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh responded with big reforms. They scrapped most licences, cut taxes on imports, welcomed foreign companies and lowered the value of the rupee. India's economy began to open up, and it grew faster in the decades that followed.

st.reveal: The RBI pledged about 47 tonnes of gold with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan to raise loans. The gold was flown out secretly, though news of it leaked and upset many Indians.

n.certNote: Historians and economists agree on what the 1991 reforms did. They still debate how much credit the reforms deserve for India's later growth, and how fairly the benefits were shared.

The reforms were largely forced by a crisis. India was close to running out of foreign money to pay for imports such as oil. The government had to act quickly, though some leaders had been arguing for changes for years.

sec.t:
After independence in 1947, India's leaders wanted to build industry quickly and keep it in Indian hands. The government ran steel plants, airlines, banks and much more. Private companies needed permission for almost everything, a system people nicknamed the "licence raj".

This protected some industries, but it also made shortages common. Waiting lists for a Bajaj scooter or a phone line could run for years. There were only a few car models, and the Ambassador and the Fiat looked the same year after year. Taxes on imports were among the highest in the world.

sec.h: A country running out of money

sec.t:
The new government acted fast. In early July, the rupee was devalued by about 18–19%, making Indian [[export|exports]] cheaper abroad. On 24 July 1991, Manmohan Singh presented a budget that changed the rules. Most industrial licences were abolished. Import duties started to fall. Foreign companies could own bigger shares of businesses in India.

He ended his speech with a line from the French writer Victor Hugo, saying that no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come. India borrowed from the IMF and the [[@world-bank-imf|World Bank]] too, and agreed to further changes as part of the deal.

Over the next decade, daily life changed in ways people could see. New car brands arrived. Telephone lines became easier to get, and then mobile phones appeared. Private airlines started flying. [[@tv-india|Cable TV]] brought dozens of channels into homes that had only Doordarshan.

Indian software companies grew quickly, selling services to the US and Europe. Cities like Bengaluru and Hyderabad became technology hubs, and later a wave of [[@indian-startups|Indian start-ups]] grew from that base. India's economy grew faster in the 2000s than in the 1970s and 80s.

The reforms are widely seen as a turning point, but not everyone agrees about their effects. Supporters point out that hundreds of millions of Indians have moved out of extreme poverty since 1991. Critics say the gains went mostly to cities and the better-off, while farmers and informal workers were left behind, and that the gap between rich and poor widened.

Some economists also note that India's growth had already started to pick up in the 1980s, so 1991 sped up a change that was beginning. What almost everyone agrees on is that the crisis of 1991 forced decisions that had been put off for years.

text: The first website was made by Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, a physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland. Its address was info.cern.ch. It went live on his computer at the end of 1990, and opened to anyone on the internet in August 1991.

The site was a few plain pages of text. It explained what the World Wide Web was, how to get a browser, and how to set up your own web server. There were no pictures, no videos and no adverts. Yet those pages started something that now reaches billions of people.

st.prompt: How many pictures did the first website have?

options.t: None, it was only text and links

st.reveal: The first website was plain black text on a white page, with blue links leading to other pages. Pictures that appear right inside a page came a couple of years later, with new web browsers.

World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), history of the Web.
Science Museum (London), Tim Berners-Lee's NeXT computer.
n.certNote: Tim Berners-Lee had his first web server running at CERN by the end of 1990. The site became open to the wider internet in August 1991, so both dates appear in histories.

myth: The internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.

The internet is the huge network of connected computers and cables, and it began in the 1960s and 70s. The Web is one service that runs on it, made of linked pages, invented in 1989–1991. Email also runs on the internet but isn't part of the Web.
facts: Tim Berners-Lee, at CERN in Switzerland
Web made free for anyone to use

sec.h: A problem at a physics lab
sec.t:
CERN is where scientists from many countries smash tiny particles together in giant machines called [[@particle-accelerators|particle accelerators]]. In the 1980s, thousands of researchers came and went, each using different computers. Sharing information was a mess.

In 1989, Berners-Lee wrote a proposal for a system of linked documents. You would click a word in one document and jump to another, even if it sat on a computer in a different country. His boss wrote "vague but exciting" on the cover. That was enough to let him carry on.

By the end of 1990, Berners-Lee had built three things that the [[@web-invented|Web]] still runs on. HTML is the language used to write web pages. URLs are the addresses, like info.cern.ch. HTTP is the set of rules computers use to send pages to each other.

He also wrote the first web browser and the first web server program. A [[server|server]] is a computer that stores pages and sends them out when someone asks. His ran on a black cube-shaped NeXT computer, which is why he stuck that warning label on it. If someone had switched it off, the whole Web would have vanished.

That computer still exists. It is kept in a museum at CERN, and an identical NeXT machine used by Berners-Lee is on show at the Science Museum in London. NeXT was the company Steve Jobs founded after he was pushed out of Apple, so the Web was born on a computer made by one of the founders of Apple.

{{story:internet-how}}

Berners-Lee could have tried to charge money for the Web. Instead, on 30 April 1993, CERN announced that anyone could use the Web's technology for free, forever. That decision helped it spread at enormous speed.

In 1993 there were a few hundred websites. By 2000 there were millions. Today there are more than a billion registered sites (2025), though most sit empty or unused and only a small share are active. It is often called one of the most generous decisions in the history of technology.

India got public internet access on 15 August 1995, when the government company VSNL launched a dial-up service. It was slow and expensive, and you heard a screech of noises as your computer connected through the phone line. Only a few thousand people signed up in the first months. Early users paid thousands of rupees a year for a connection, and loading a single page with pictures could take minutes.

Today India has hundreds of millions of internet users, many using phones rather than computers, and the story of how that happened is told in [[@internet-india|the internet in India]].

The original pages changed often, and no copy of the very first version survives. In 2013, CERN rebuilt the earliest copy it could find, from 1992, and put it back at info.cern.ch. You can visit it and click the old blue links today. Finding a single page among the billions out there now needs a whole new tool, a [[@search-engines|search engine]], which the first Web didn't have at all.

text: Kanyakumari is a small town at the very southern tip of mainland India, in Tamil Nadu. Here the Arabian Sea to the west, the Bay of Bengal to the east and the Indian Ocean to the south all meet. Hindus call this meeting point a sangam, and many pilgrims bathe there.

Because the land narrows to a point, the sea lies to the east, south and west. That makes Kanyakumari one of the few places in India where you can watch both sunrise and sunset over water. Out in the waves stand two rocky islets, one topped by a memorial to Swami Vivekananda and the other by a giant statue of the Tamil poet Thiruvalluvar.

options.t: It matches the depth of the sea around the rock

st.reveal: The poet Thiruvalluvar's book, the Thirukkural, has 133 chapters of ten couplets each. The statue is 95 feet tall on a 38-foot pedestal, adding up to 133.

myth: You can see three different coloured seas meeting in neat stripes at Kanyakumari.
The three bodies of water flow into each other without clear lines. On some days, currents, sand and light make patches of slightly different colour, which is where the idea comes from.

Glass bridge between rock and statue

sec.t:
The town takes its name from Kanya Kumari, the virgin goddess, a form of the goddess Parvati. Her temple stands near the shore. In the best-known legend, she was to marry the god Shiva at midnight. When the wedding did not happen, she remained unmarried, waiting at the tip of India forever. Some versions say the rice and grains for the wedding feast turned into the multicoloured sand found on the beach.

Pilgrims from all over India visit the temple. People of many faiths come to see the sunrise.

On the neighbouring rock stands a statue of Thiruvalluvar, author of the [[@thirukkural|Thirukkural]], a book of 1,330 short [[couplet|couplets]] about good living, wealth and love. The statue was unveiled on the first day of 2000. Its total height, 133 feet, stands for the 133 chapters of his book. It was built to stand up to storms and survived the 2004 [[tsunami|tsunami]], which killed many people along this coast.

Since December 2024, a glass-floored bridge about 77 metres long has linked the two rocks. Visitors walk across with the waves visible beneath their feet.

sec.h: Sunrise, sunset and a full moon
sec.t:
Crowds gather on the beach before dawn. As the sun clears the horizon, cameras click and tea sellers do brisk business. In the evening, people move to Sunset Point on the western side.

On Chitra Pournami, the full moon of the Tamil month of Chithirai in April or May, there is a rarer sight. Sometimes the moon rises over one sea while the sun sets over another, both visible at once. The orange [[@colour-of-sky-sunset|sunset]] and the pale moon face each other across the sky.

sec.h: Gandhi's ashes and a beam of sun
sec.t:
After Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] died in 1948, part of his ashes were kept at Kanyakumari before being scattered in the sea. The Gandhi Mandapam was built on the spot. It was designed so that on 2 October, his birthday, sunlight falls through a hole in the roof onto the place where the urn stood.

Look at a map of [[@india-geography|India's shape]] and Kanyakumari is its sharp point. Sail due south from here and, after about 5,000 km of open ocean, the first land is a tiny French island called Île Amsterdam. Keep going and the next stop is Antarctica.

text: The Meenakshi Temple, also called Meenakshi Amman Temple or Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple, is a huge Hindu temple in the city of Madurai, in Tamil Nadu. It is dedicated to the goddess Meenakshi, a form of Parvati, and her husband Sundareswarar, a form of Shiva.

The temple covers about 6 hectares, around the size of eight football fields, and is surrounded by high walls. Fourteen towering gateways, called gopurams, rise above it, covered in brightly painted statues. Inside are halls, shrines, a sacred tank and long corridors of carved pillars. Thousands of people visit every day, and the old city of Madurai is built in squares around it.

st.prompt: How many pillars are there in the Meenakshi Temple's Hall of a Thousand Pillars?
st.reveal: The hall has 985 carved pillars, arranged in rows so that from many spots they seem to line up perfectly. "Thousand" is a round number that sounds grander, a bit like saying "a million things to do".

Encyclopaedia Britannica, Madurai.
George Michell, The Hindu Temple (1977).
n.certNote: The temple is very old, and Tamil poems mention a temple in Madurai many centuries ago. Most of the buildings standing today, though, date from the 1500s and 1600s, and historians debate how much of the earlier temple survives.

sec.t:
The name Meenakshi means "the one with fish-shaped eyes", a way of saying her eyes were beautiful. According to the temple's legend, she was born to a Pandya king of Madurai. She grew up a fearless warrior and ruled the kingdom herself, conquering lands in every direction.

When she reached Mount Kailash and met Shiva, the story says, she fell in love. Shiva came to Madurai as Sundareswarar, "the beautiful lord", and married her. Every year, in the Tamil month of Chithirai, around April or May, the city celebrates their wedding in a festival that draws huge crowds.

Gopurams are the gateway towers of south Indian temples. The Meenakshi Temple has 14. The tallest, on the southern side, is about 52 m high, roughly as tall as a 17-storey building.

Every gopuram is covered in painted figures of gods, goddesses, demons, animals and characters from Hindu stories. They're made of stucco, a kind of plaster, over a frame of brick. The paint fades in the sun and rain, so the towers are repainted every few years during restoration. Each repainting is done by traditional craftspeople, and it can take many months.

In the middle of the temple is the Potramarai Kulam, the "golden lotus tank", with a gilded lotus at its centre. Steps lead down to the water on all sides.

A legend links it to the Tamil Sangam, the ancient gathering of poets. It's said that new works were placed on the water to be judged. Good poems floated, while poor ones sank. Nobody takes that as history, but it shows how proud Madurai was of its poets.

The Hall of a Thousand Pillars is a great hall with 985 carved stone pillars, built in the 1500s. From many spots inside, the rows of pillars seem to line up perfectly. Today it houses a museum of temple art.

Some pillars in the temple are musical. Tap them gently and they ring with different notes, because of their size and shape. [[@sound-travel|Sound]] travels through solid stone, and each column vibrates in its own way. Visitors are asked not to tap them, to protect the carvings.

Old Madurai grew around the temple in rings of square streets. Several are named after Tamil months, such as Chithirai Street and Masi Street, because festival processions pass along them in those months.

Every evening, an image of Sundareswarar is carried in a procession to Meenakshi's shrine, to rest there for the night. In the morning, the temple wakes again to bells, drums and the smell of jasmine sold by the flower sellers at its gates.

text: As of 2024, Indonesia's government counts 17,380 islands. That makes it the largest country made entirely of islands, an [[archipelago|archipelago]]. Its official number has changed over the years, because counting islands is harder than it sounds. Some appear only at low tide, some are tiny rocks, and new surveys keep finding more. Each island must be named, measured and checked by experts before it is counted, and newly verified islands are still being added to the official records.

Most islands are small and empty. People live on perhaps a few thousand of them. The biggest, like Sumatra, Java, Borneo and Sulawesi, hold most of the country's roughly 280 million people. Java alone is home to more than half of them, packed onto an island a little smaller than the Indian state of Odisha.

st.reveal: About 280 million people lived in Indonesia in 2024, making it the fourth most populous country after India, China and the USA. More than half of them live on just one island, Java.

sec.t:
Indonesia sits where several of Earth's huge [[plate|plates]] push against each other. As one plate slides under another, rock melts and rises, building chains of [[@volcano|volcanoes]]. Over millions of years, many of those volcanoes grew into islands.

The country has about 130 active volcanoes, more than almost anywhere else. They make the soil rich for farming but also cause earthquakes and eruptions. In 2004, an undersea earthquake off Sumatra set off the [[tsunami|tsunami]] that also struck India's coasts.

In 1883, the volcano Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, blew itself apart. The sound was heard about 4,800 km away, on Rodrigues Island in the Indian Ocean. It may be the loudest sound in recorded history. Ash in the sky turned sunsets red around the world for months.

Far bigger was Toba, on Sumatra, about 74,000 years ago. It was one of the largest eruptions of the last few million years. Its ash fell as far as India. The [[crater|crater]] it left is now Lake Toba, about 100 km long, with an island inside it about the size of Singapore.

Ships crossed the Indian Ocean between India and Indonesia for more than 1,500 years. Traders carried spices, cloth and ideas, and Hindu and Buddhist kingdoms grew on Sumatra and Java. The sea [[empire|empire]] of [[@srivijaya|Srivijaya]] became a famous centre of Buddhist learning.

On Java stands [[@borobudur|Borobudur]], a huge Buddhist monument from the 800s. Nearby, the Hindu temples of Prambanan are carved with scenes from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], which dancers still perform there on moonlit nights. Most Indonesians today are Muslim, making it the country with the most Muslims in the world. Bali remains mostly Hindu.

Indonesia has more than 700 languages. To help everyone understand each other, the country uses one national language, Bahasa Indonesia, taught in all schools. Many Indonesians speak a local language at home and the national one at school.

Jakarta, the capital on Java, is so crowded and sinking so fast that the government has been building a new capital, Nusantara, on Borneo. And India is closer than you might think. Indira Point, at the southern tip of the [[@andaman|Andaman and Nicobar Islands]], is less than 200 km of sea from the Indonesian island of Sumatra.
